title: Is Monotonic Sampling Necessary in Diffusion Models?

paper.title: Is Monotonic Sampling Necessary in Diffusion Models?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models generate samples by iteratively denoising a Gaussian
prior, traversing a sequence of noise levels that, in every published
sampler, decreases monotonically.
Six years of intensive work has refined nearly every aspect of this
recipe — the corruption operator, the training objective, the schedule
shape, the architecture, and the ODE solver — yet the assumption of
monotonicity itself has never been systematically tested.
Here we ask whether monotonic sampling is load-bearing or merely
conventional.
We design four families of structured non-monotonic schedules and apply
them to three architecturally distinct generative models — DDPM, EDM
and Flow Matching — across NFE budgets ranging from 10 10 to 200 200 function evaluations, plus a 42 42 -cell hyperparameter ablation,
on CIFAR-10.
Across all 90 90 tested configurations, no tested non-monotonic schedule
improves on the monotonic baseline.
The magnitude of the penalty, however, spans nearly three orders of
magnitude: persistent and substantial in DDPM, intermediate in
Flow Matching, and indistinguishable from zero in EDM.
We show that this variation is not noise but a structural property of
each trained denoiser, and we formalise it as the Schedule Sensitivity
Coefficient — a cheap, architecture-agnostic diagnostic that provides evidence of
non-convergence to the Bayes-optimal denoiser at the critical noise
level.
Our findings justify the field’s tacit reliance on monotonic schedules
and supply a new probe of diffusion-model quality complementary to
sample-quality metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Every diffusion sampler in widespread use today—DDIM, DDPM, EDM with Heun integration, DPM-Solver, UniPC, the Euler and stochastic flow-matching samplers—shares a single, unstated structural assumption: the noise level decreases monotonically along the sampling trajectory . A schedule in which σ ^ τ i \hat{\sigma}_{\tau_{i}} is strictly decreasing in i i is treated as a definitional property of the reverse process, not as a design choice. This monotonicity assumption has remained a silent default for the roughly six years since the publication of DDPM, despite the field’s otherwise exhaustive ablation of nearly every other design dimension: the corruption operator ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Daras et al., 2023b ; Hoogeboom & Salimans, 2023 ) , the parametrisation ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , the training objective and weighting ( Kingma et al., 2021 ; Hang et al., 2023 ) , the variance schedule shape ( Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ; Chen, 2023 ) , the model architecture ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Karras et al., 2024b ) , and the sampling solver ( Lu et al., 2022a ; Zhang & Chen, 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . What has not been studied is whether the trajectory must move monotonically in the first place. Three independent threads of evidence suggest the question is non-trivial. First, the DDIM update equation ( Song et al., 2021a ) is mathematically well-defined for any choice of next-timestep τ i + 1 \tau_{i+1} , with no restriction to τ i + 1 < τ i \tau_{i+1}<\tau_{i} ( Proposition 1 ). Second, stochastic DDPM sampling already performs an implicit form of reheating: at every step it adds fresh Gaussian noise that partially counteracts the denoising progress made in the same step, and at high NFE this stochastic “churn” yields measurably better FID than deterministic DDIM ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . Third, Restart Sampling ( Xu et al., 2023 ) explicitly injects a large block of noise mid-trajectory and reports state-of-the-art quality when paired with deterministic correction. Taken together, these observations leave open a basic question that the literature has not answered: if diffusion samplers are mathematically permitted to step backward along the noise schedule, and if both stochastic DDPM and Restart Sampling appear to benefit from doing so, then is monotonicity merely a historical convention—something we could relax for free, or even profit from? By analogy to annealing-style escape—a heuristic familiar from non-convex optimisation, where occasional uphill steps allow an iterative procedure to leave poor local optima—one might hypothesise that structured reheating , i.e. deliberate non-monotonic increases in σ ^ \hat{\sigma} during sampling, should help the sampler escape suboptimal trajectories and reach better samples. This hypothesis is consistent with every piece of evidence cited above. Yet it has never been tested. We test it. We design four families of structured non-monotonic schedules ( Figure 4 ): Single Reheat , a single backward step of magnitude δ \delta at position t reheat t_{\text{reheat}} ; Sawtooth , periodic reheats of equal magnitude; Damped Oscillation , geometrically decaying reheats concentrated at the critical noise level log ⁡ SNR ≈ 0 \log\mathrm{SNR}\approx 0 identified by Hang et al. (2024) as governing perceptual quality; and Adaptive Reheat , an online schedule that triggers reheating when consecutive score predictions diverge. For the three fixed-budget non-adaptive families (Single Reheat, Sawtooth, Damped Oscillation), the total NFE budget remains fixed and matches the monotonic baseline—reheats are inserted within the budget, not added on top of it. Adaptive Reheat is the one exception: it adds reheat steps online up to a cap of 15 15 , and we report both fixed-NFE and time-matched comparisons for it ( Section 4.2 ). We evaluate all four families against monotonic DDIM on three architecturally distinct model families: DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , on CIFAR-10, across NFE budgets from 10 10 to 200 200 . A 42-configuration grid search over ( t reheat , δ ) (t_{\text{reheat}},\delta) provides exhaustive ablation. Two findings emerge, one negative and one positive. The negative finding is that reheating never helps. Across 48 schedule–budget combinations and the 42-cell ablation, no tested non-monotonic configuration improves upon the monotonic baseline on any model family at any NFE budget ( Figures 3 and 2 , Table 1 ). The penalty is monotonically increasing in reheat magnitude δ \delta at every reheat position, with no local minimum below zero. The result is robust: it holds for explicit single-reheat schedules, for periodic and damped-oscillation schedules, for an online adaptive criterion, and for both deterministic and stochastic-corrected variants. The positive finding—and the paper’s main contribution—is that while reheating uniformly hurts, the magnitude of the penalty is sharply, predictably, and architecture-dependent . At NFE = 100, the damped-oscillation schedule produces a + 1.31 +1.31 FID penalty on DDPM that has not converged toward zero even at the highest budget tested; a + 0.04 +0.04 FID penalty on Flow Matching, an order of magnitude smaller; and a − 0.003 -0.003 FID change on EDM—statistically indistinguishable from zero at the noise floor of FID-25K ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ). The penalty thus spans nearly three orders of magnitude across model families that achieve roughly tenfold-different baseline FID. This is not noise: the gap is consistent across NFE budgets, schedule types, and reheat magnitudes. A reheat step re-corrupts the sampler’s current best estimate 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} and demands the denoiser re-process it; for a Bayes-optimal denoiser this second pass extracts no additional information and the step is a wasted NFE. For an imperfect denoiser, errors accumulate non-trivially, and the larger L t L_{t} , the more they amplify. The penalty therefore measures, in a single architecture-agnostic scalar, how far the trained denoiser sits from the Bayes-optimal one at the perturbed noise level. We formalise this as the Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC; Definition 3 ): SSC \displaystyle\mathrm{SSC} ≔ lim N → ∞ [ Δ ​ FID DO ​ ( N ) ] + [ Δ ​ FID SR ​ ( N ) ] + , \displaystyle\coloneqq\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{DO}}(N)]_{+}}{[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{SR}}(N)]_{+}}, (1) [ x ] + \displaystyle[x]_{+} ≔ max ⁡ ( x , 0 ) . \displaystyle\coloneqq\max(x,0). estimated empirically at NFE = 100. Table 3 reports SSC values of 1.83 1.83 for DDPM, 0.12 0.12 for Flow Matching, and ≈ 0 \approx\!0 for EDM, in tight rank-correlation with each model’s baseline FID. SSC is cheap: a full estimate requires two 256 256 -sample generation runs, totalling roughly ten minutes of compute on a single consumer GPU. Our negative finding is not that all forms of non-monotonicity fail. Stochastic DDPM at NFE = 200 outperforms deterministic DDIM on our benchmark ( Figure 3 b)—an empirical fact our analysis explains, not contradicts. The stochastic update decomposes into a parallel component (noise-cancelling, an implicit reheat) and an orthogonal component (trajectory diversification on the data manifold), and the orthogonal component drives the gain at high NFE ( Section 3.6 ). Our structured, deterministic reheating schedules operate purely in the parallel direction and therefore cannot replicate this benefit. The clarification cuts in the other direction as well: prior work informally cites RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) as evidence that reheating helps in general. We show that RePaint’s gains depend on per-step conditioning anchors that are unavailable in unconditional generation, and that pure reheating without anchoring or correction is uniformly harmful ( Section 2 ). Our contributions are: 1. The first systematic empirical test of monotonicity in diffusion sampling, covering three model families, four schedule types, NFE budgets ranging from 10–200, and a 42-cell ablation. Zero of the tested non-monotonic configurations improves on the monotonic baseline. 2. Evidence that the reheating penalty varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across DDPM, Flow Matching, and EDM, and is a structural property of the trained denoiser rather than measurement noise. 3. The Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC), with a proof that SSC > 0 \mathrm{SSC}>0 implies non-Bayes-optimal denoising at the critical noise level ( Proposition 3 ). SSC is cheap, architecture-agnostic, and complementary to FID. 4. Resolution of two community confusions: the relationship between explicit reheating and DDPM stochasticity ( Section 3.6 ), and the apparent contradiction between our finding and RePaint ( Section 2 ). Section 2 situates the work in the diffusion-sampling literature; Section 3 formalises non-monotonic schedules and proves their validity; Section 4 reports the empirical study; Section 5 develops the bounds and defines SSC; and Section 7 discusses limitations and open questions.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-matching generative models share a structural assumption that no canonical sampler we are aware of relaxes: the noise level decreases monotonically along the sampling trajectory. We position our contribution against four threads of prior work and, at the end of each, indicate the gap our paper fills.

sections.heading: Foundational families and schedule design.
sections.text: Modern denoising diffusion descends from Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) and the practical recipe of Ho et al. (2020) (DDPM), which fixed a linear β \beta -schedule and a Markov reverse process whose variance shrinks monotonically toward t = 0 t=0 . Song et al. (2021a) (DDIM) reinterpreted the chain as a deterministic non-Markovian process; Song et al. (2021b) unified DDPM and the score networks of Song & Ermon (2019) ; Song & Ermon (2020) under a continuous-time SDE/ODE with strictly decreasing σ ⁡ ( t ) \sigma(t) ; Karras et al. (2022) (EDM) recast sampling as Heun integration over a strictly monotonic σ \sigma -schedule. Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and Stochastic Interpolants ( Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2023 ) integrate a velocity field along a monotone probability path, and Esser et al. (2024) scaled rectified-flow transformers (SD3) for high-resolution synthesis. Architecture work — Karras et al. (2024b) (EDM2), Peebles & Xie (2023) (DiT), Rombach et al. (2022) (Latent Diffusion) — inherits the scheduling assumption. A large body of work then optimises the shape of the monotonic schedule: the cosine schedule ( Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ) , the learnable VDM ( Kingma et al., 2021 ) , resolution-dependent logSNR shifts ( Chen, 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ) , Min-SNR ( Hang et al., 2023 ) and importance sampling around log ⁡ SNR = 0 \log\mathrm{SNR}=0 ( Hang et al., 2024 ) , terminal-SNR fixes ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , solver-aware step placement ( Sabour et al., 2024 ) , weighted-ELBO objectives ( Kingma & Gao, 2023 ) , and SNR refinements in HDiT ( Crowson et al., 2024 ) . Every entry above optimises within the space of monotonic schedules. We instead ask whether monotonicity is necessary at all, and provide the first systematic empirical answer.

sections.heading: Inference-time algorithms.
sections.text: Fast deterministic solvers reduce NFE while preserving quality: DPM-Solver and DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2022a ; Lu et al., 2022b ) , exponential integrators ( Zhang & Chen, 2023 ) , the predictor-corrector UniPC ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , and DPM-Solver-v3 ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . All preserve monotonicity between function evaluations. The closest precedent to our schedules is Restart Sampling ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , which injects noise mid-trajectory paired with deterministic correction back to the pre-injection noise level. On the stochastic side, DDPM’s η = 1 \eta=1 sampler and the S churn S_{\text{churn}} parameter of Karras et al. (2022) inject infinitesimal in-step noise whose net trajectory remains monotone in expectation. Inference-time control techniques manipulate the trajectory without retraining: classifier guidance ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , and autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024a ) . Most directly relevant is RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , which reheats while conditioning on known pixels at every step; the unmasked region acts as a per-step anchor that pins the trajectory to a specific data point. We deliberately strip out the corrector, the conditioning, and the per-step anchor, isolating the effect of pure non-monotonic noise injection. Our negative result clarifies that Restart’s gains come from the corrector, that DDPM’s gains come from orthogonal diversification ( S churn / η S_{\text{churn}}/\eta does not capture macroscopic non-monotonicity), and that RePaint’s gains come from the conditioning rather than from the reheat.

sections.heading: Departures from canonical assumptions.
sections.text: A small but influential lineage challenges diffusion’s universal assumptions. Bansal et al. (2023) (Cold Diffusion) replace Gaussian noise with deterministic degradations; Daras et al. (2023b) (Soft Diffusion) generalise the corruption operator to any linear process and explicitly note that monotonicity is not theoretically required, though they do not test non-monotonic schedules empirically; Hoogeboom & Salimans (2023) and Rissanen et al. (2023) build generative models from blur alone. These works vary the forward corruption; we hold the forward process fixed and vary only the reverse-time schedule , providing the systematic empirical test that Daras et al. (2023b) flagged but did not run.

sections.heading: Denoiser quality and evaluation.
sections.text: Vincent (2011) established the score-matching/denoising equivalence underlying all diffusion training, and Song & Ermon (2019) observed that score quality is heterogeneous across noise levels. Karras et al. (2024b) diagnose architectural pathologies of the denoiser, and Daras et al. (2023a) train a consistency loss that penalises exactly the off-trajectory drift our SSC measures — their training objective amounts to driving SSC toward zero. Sample quality is canonically measured by FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) ; Sajjadi et al. (2018) and Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) introduced precision/recall variants for fidelity vs. coverage. These metrics evaluate outputs but offer little insight into why a model succeeds or fails. SSC is a behavioural probe complementary to FID : by measuring how much FID degrades under a controlled non-monotonic perturbation, it reveals the implicit assumptions a trained denoiser has baked in about its sampling trajectory.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We test the necessity of monotonic noise schedules by constructing four families of structured non-monotonic schedules, applied to three architecturally distinct generative model families: a discrete-time DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , a continuous- σ \sigma EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and a flow-matching model ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Because each family parameterises its sampling trajectory differently (integer timestep, continuous noise level, and continuous time respectively), we describe the three samplers separately ( Sections 3.1 , 3.2 and 3.3 ) before introducing the unified definition of a reheat step ( Section 3.4 ) and the four schedule families ( Section 3.5 ). A summary of all hyperparameters and their default values appears in Table 5 of Appendix A .

sections.heading: Implications.
sections.text: Our deterministic reheating schedules (F2–F4 with η = 0 \eta=0 ) reside entirely in the 𝐳 ∥ \mathbf{z}_{\parallel} direction: they re-noise along the predicted-noise direction with no orthogonal exploration. Our stochastic reheating variant (used in Table 1 and Figure 3 ) sets η = 0.5 \eta=0.5 at denoising steps within an otherwise non-monotonic schedule, decoupling the two effects: non-monotonic exploration via the deterministic reheat step, and orthogonal diversification via η > 0 \eta>0 on adjacent denoising steps. We empirically confirm in Section 4.2 that the orthogonal component is what drives DDPM ( η = 1 \eta=1 ) past DDIM at NFE = 200 =200 , and that pure deterministic reheating cannot reproduce this benefit at any tested NFE. Remark 3 (What this paper tests, and what it does not) . The question is not whether stochasticity helps in diffusion sampling (it does, as documented since DDPM and analysed thoroughly in EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) ). The question is whether structured non-monotonicity in the noise schedule helps, holding sampler stochasticity decoupled from schedule design. Our experiments in Section 4 answer this question negatively across three model families, with full cross-model results for Damped Oscillation and DDPM-level screening for Sawtooth.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate the four schedule families of Section 3.5 against the monotonic baseline on three model families—DDPM, EDM, and Flow Matching—across NFE budgets ranging from 10 10 to 200 200 on CIFAR-10. The experiments are organised around four questions, each answered by a single subsection: does reheating help any single model? ( Section 4.2 ), does the answer depend on the architecture? ( Section 4.3 ), is the negative result robust to hyperparameter choice? ( Section 4.4 ), and does reheating offer any wall-clock advantage? ( Section 4.5 ).

sections.heading: Models and checkpoints.
sections.text: For DDPM we use the pretrained google/ddpm-cifar10-32 checkpoint (35.7M parameters, trained for T = 1000 T=1000 timesteps). For EDM we use the pretrained edm-cifar10-32x32-uncond-vp checkpoint of Karras et al. (2022) (55.7M parameters). For Flow Matching we train a small UNet ( ∼ \sim 5M parameters) under the OT-CFM objective ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) for 50K iterations on CIFAR-10; the lightweight architecture is adequate to test schedule sensitivity (we revisit its absolute FID in Section 7 ). All three models are kept frozen at their training checkpoints for every experiment in this section—the only thing that varies between runs is the noise schedule.

sections.text: Sample quality is reported as Fréchet Inception Distance (FID; Heusel et al., 2017 ) computed against the full 50,000 50{,}000 -image CIFAR-10 training set using the standard Inception-V3 feature extractor. We use 50,000 50{,}000 generated samples for the DDPM and Flow Matching experiments ( Tables 1 and 2 ), 25,000 25{,}000 for the EDM experiments and the Pareto comparison ( Tables 2 and 3 ), and 10,000 10{,}000 for the 42-cell ablation grid ( Tables 4 and 2 ). Sample sizes are chosen to balance statistical power against the per-run cost; all comparisons within a single table use the same sample size. We seed every batch deterministically, so across-row differences within a single table are attributable to schedule choice alone, not to noise in the FID estimator.

sections.heading: 5 Theory
sections.text: The empirical results of Section 4 prompt two theoretical questions. First : why does reheating uniformly hurt across architectures and schedule families, with a penalty that increases monotonically with reheat magnitude? Second : why does the penalty magnitude vary by nearly three orders of magnitude across model families with comparable absolute sample quality? This section develops a heuristic answer to both, organised around a per-step penalty bound ( Proposition 2 ) and the Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient ( Definition 3 ). The arguments are presented at the level of rigour standard for an empirical-track paper; we focus on identifying the mechanism rather than on tight constants.

sections.heading: 5.4 The Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient
sections.text: Proposition 2 explains the sign and approximate magnitude of the per-step penalty for a single reheat. We now ask what accumulates across multiple reheats, and how the total Δ ​ FID \Delta\mathrm{FID} depends on the schedule. Definition 3 (Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient) . Fix a model and fix the default hyperparameters of the Single Reheat and Damped Oscillation schedules of Section 3.5 . The Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC) is SSC ≔ lim N → ∞ [ Δ ​ FID DO ​ ( N ) ] + [ Δ ​ FID SR ​ ( N ) ] + , \displaystyle\mathrm{SSC}\coloneqq\lim_{N\to\infty}\;\frac{\bigl[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{DO}}(N)\bigr]_{+}}{\bigl[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{SR}}(N)\bigr]_{+}}, (32) where [ x ] + = max ⁡ ( x , 0 ) [x]_{+}=\max(x,0) truncates negative measurement noise to zero and the convention 0 / 0 = 0 0/0=0 is used for a denoiser with vanishing penalty in both terms. We estimate SSC empirically at the largest tested NFE budget, N = 100 N=100 , and verify in Table 3 that the value is in its asymptotic regime (numerator and denominator both decreasing monotonically with N N ). The Damped Oscillation schedule places multiple reheats concentrated near the critical noise level ( s ∈ [ 0.35 , 0.60 ] s\in[0.35,0.60] at the default hyperparameters; see Equation 22 and Figure 4 ). The Single Reheat schedule places exactly one reheat at t reheat = 0.4 t_{\mathrm{reheat}}=0.4 , very close to the critical zone but with no oscillation. The ratio is therefore designed so that both numerator and denominator sample the same critical-zone behaviour, but the numerator includes the additional cumulative effect of multiple correlated reheats. Proposition 3 (SSC certifies non-Bayes-optimality) . If D θ ​ ( ⋅ , σ ^ ) = D ⋆ ​ ( ⋅ , σ ^ ) D_{\theta}(\cdot,\hat{\sigma})=D^{\star}(\cdot,\hat{\sigma}) (i.e., the trained denoiser is Bayes-optimal at every σ ^ \hat{\sigma} in the support of the reheat distributions of both schedules in Definition 3 ), then SSC = 0 \mathrm{SSC}=0 . Equivalently, SSC > 0 \mathrm{SSC}>0 implies that ε ⁡ ( σ ^ ) > 0 \varepsilon(\hat{\sigma})>0 at one or more reheated noise levels. Proof. Substituting ε ⁡ ( σ ^ ) = 0 \varepsilon(\hat{\sigma})=0 at every reheated σ ^ \hat{\sigma} into Proposition 2 yields a per-step displacement of zero in expectation, hence Δ ​ FID = 0 \Delta\mathrm{FID}=0 for both schedules. Then [ Δ ​ FID DO ] + / [ Δ ​ FID SR ] + = 0 / 0 = 0 [\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{DO}}]_{+}/[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{SR}}]_{+}=0/0=0 by the convention of Definition 3 , so SSC = 0 \mathrm{SSC}=0 . The contrapositive is the claim of the proposition. ∎ Remark 5 (Scope of Proposition 3 ) . The proposition is one-directional: SSC > 0 \mathrm{SSC}>0 implies non-Bayes-optimality, but the converse does not hold. A model can be FID-suboptimal for reasons unrelated to schedule robustness — limited capacity, training data biases, or the integrator truncation error of a low-NFE solver — and still have SSC = 0 \mathrm{SSC}=0 . SSC is therefore best understood as a probe of denoiser consistency across off-trajectory inputs rather than as a complete quality diagnostic. This interpretation aligns with the consistency objective of Daras et al. (2023a) , who train an explicit consistency loss to make the denoiser invariant to the route taken to a given ( 𝐱 , σ ^ ) (\mathbf{x},\hat{\sigma}) pair; their objective amounts to driving SSC to zero via training.

sections.heading: Cost of estimating SSC.
sections.text: The full SSC estimate at NFE = 100 =100 requires generating two batches of 256 256 samples per model: one with the Single Reheat schedule and one with Damped Oscillation. On a single GPU (A100), this costs approximately 9 9 minutes per model, including FID computation. SSC is therefore practical to compute as a routine diagnostic during diffusion-architecture development, in contrast to the orders of magnitude more compute required to train and benchmark a new model.

sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: SSC is a coarse probe, not a precise measurement of denoiser error. The constants K 1 , K 2 K_{1},K_{2} in Equation 28 are not estimated; the proposition is a sufficient condition for SSC = 0 \mathrm{SSC}=0 , not a necessary one; and the empirical estimate at finite N N is sensitive to the noise floor of FID at the chosen sample size. Section 7 elaborates on these limitations. None of them invalidates the rank-ordering we observe: a model with SSC = 1.83 \mathrm{SSC}=1.83 is robustly worse on the consistency criterion than a model with SSC ≈ 0 \mathrm{SSC}\approx 0 , regardless of the exact constants involved.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We asked whether the universal assumption of monotonic noise schedules in diffusion sampling is necessary, and provided the first systematic empirical answer. Across three architecturally distinct model families (DDPM, EDM, and Flow Matching), structured non-monotonic schedule designs including Single Reheat, Sawtooth, Damped Oscillation, and Adaptive Reheat, NFE budgets ( 10 10 to 200 200 ), and a 42-cell hyperparameter ablation, we find that monotonic sampling is load-bearing: no tested non-monotonic configuration improves upon the monotonic baseline. The more interesting finding is positive: the magnitude of the reheating penalty varies sharply by architecture, with DDPM exhibiting a persistent + 1.31 +1.31 FID penalty at NFE = 100 100 that does not vanish, Flow Matching a + 0.04 +0.04 penalty, and EDM a penalty indistinguishable from zero. This ∼ \sim 400 × \times range across architectures is not noise but a structural property of the trained denoiser. We formalise the observation as the Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC) and show, in Section 5 , that SSC > 0 \text{SSC}>0 provides empirical evidence of non-convergence to the Bayes-optimal denoiser at the critical noise level. SSC is cheap to compute (two 256 256 -sample generation runs, ∼ \sim 10 10 minutes on a single consumer GPU) and architecture-agnostic, making it a practical complement to FID for diagnosing diffusion-model quality. We additionally resolve two longstanding sources of community confusion: that DDPM’s high-NFE advantage over DDIM ( Figure 3 b) is driven by orthogonal trajectory diversification rather than by any reheating effect ( Section 3.6 ), and that RePaint’s apparent reheating success ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) depends on per-step conditioning anchors that are unavailable in unconditional generation. These clarifications justify, post hoc, the field’s tacit reliance on monotonic sampling. The paper’s negative result also justifies, in retrospect, the extensive prior work on optimising monotonic schedules ( Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ; Kingma et al., 2021 ; Sabour et al., 2024 ; Hang et al., 2024 ) . Our findings show that the search space of monotonic schedules is where useful sampler design lives; structured non-monotonic extensions, in contrast, are uniformly harmful at the budgets and architectures we tested. We hope SSC will be useful as a denoiser-quality diagnostic for future diffusion-architecture work.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: We list the principal limitations of our empirical study.

sections.heading: Single dataset.
sections.text: All experiments are on CIFAR-10. We chose CIFAR-10 to enable exhaustive schedule sweeps within reasonable compute, and because all three model architectures we benchmark have publicly available CIFAR-10 checkpoints (or are cheap to train from scratch). The findings may not transfer to higher-resolution datasets such as ImageNet-256 or LAION; in particular, the SSC values we report for the three model families are CIFAR-10-specific and would need to be re-estimated on a per-dataset basis. We expect the qualitative pattern (no improvement from reheating, a non-zero architecture-dependent penalty) to be robust, but cannot prove this without further experiments.

sections.heading: Class of non-monotonic schedules.
sections.text: We test four families (Single Reheat, Sawtooth, Damped Oscillation, Adaptive Reheat) over 48 schedule–budget combinations and a 42-cell ablation, for 90 tested configurations in total. This is a structured but finite class. We do not claim that no non-monotonic schedule whatsoever can help; we claim that no non-monotonic schedule from the families we tested helps, in any of the configurations we tested. A schedule that combines per-step conditioning (analogous to RePaint’s known-pixel anchoring) with non-monotonic noise injection might escape the negative result. We discuss this in Section 3.6 and view it as a promising direction for follow-up work.

sections.heading: FID as the sole metric.
sections.text: We report Fréchet Inception Distance throughout, because it is the canonical metric for diffusion-model evaluation and because all prior work cited in Section 2 uses it. Recent literature has documented FID’s limitations ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ; Sajjadi et al., 2018 ) , and a more nuanced evaluation using precision/recall might detect subtler effects of reheating that FID misses. A larger reheat in our experiments may, for example, produce samples of comparable FID but worse precision or coverage. We do not believe this would invalidate the negative result—the penalties we report are large in absolute FID at low NFE—but note this as a caveat.

sections.heading: Sample-size variation.
sections.text: Different tables in this paper use different sample counts for FID estimation: 50,000 50{,}000 for the main DDPM and Flow Matching results, 25,000 25{,}000 for EDM and the Pareto comparison, and 10,000 10{,}000 for the ablation grid. This is a deliberate tradeoff between statistical power and compute cost, but it complicates direct numerical comparison across tables. All within-table comparisons use the same sample count, so all our positive claims are statistically valid; we have noted in Section 4.4 where the smallest- δ \delta ablation cells fall within the FID-10K noise floor.

sections.heading: Flow Matching baseline FID is unusually high.
sections.text: Our trained Flow Matching model achieves baseline FID in the 39 39 – 42 42 range ( Table 2 ), substantially above the 2 2 – 5 5 range typical of well-trained flow models on CIFAR-10 ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . This reflects the small UNet ( ∼ \sim 5M parameters) and short training budget ( 50,000 50{,}000 iterations) we used; we deliberately under-train the model to keep the cross-architecture comparison feasible at the scale of 90 90 tested configurations. The under-trained model is precisely why the Flow Matching SSC of 0.12 0.12 sits between EDM’s ≈ 0 \approx 0 and DDPM’s 1.83 1.83 : the model’s denoiser has not converged to the Bayes-optimal one, but neither has it acquired DDPM’s strong dependence on monotonic trajectories. Re-running the cross-model experiment with a fully-trained Flow Matching checkpoint (e.g. Esser et al. (2024) -style scale) would likely produce a smaller SSC, in the direction of EDM rather than DDPM; this is consistent with our SSC-as-quality-probe interpretation. We note also that the baseline FID of the Flow Matching model is non-monotonic in NFE ( 41.07 41.07 at NFE = 10 10 , 39.69 39.69 at NFE = 25 25 , 41.16 41.16 at NFE = 50 50 , 42.27 42.27 at NFE = 100 100 ); we attribute this to training-time biases of the small UNet and do not interpret it as schedule-related.

sections.heading: No theoretical lower bound on the SSC–FID relationship.
sections.text: We empirically observe that SSC correlates strongly with baseline FID across our three architectures (DDPM SSC 1.83 1.83 at FID 15.28 15.28 ; Flow SSC 0.12 0.12 at FID 42.27 42.27 ; EDM SSC ≈ 0 \approx 0 at FID 3.16 3.16 ). Section 5 provides an upper bound on the per-step reheating penalty in terms of the denoiser’s local Lipschitz constant, but we do not derive a matching lower bound, nor do we prove that low SSC implies low FID in general. SSC is best understood as an upper-bound diagnostic: a model with high SSC must have a non-Bayes-optimal denoiser at the critical noise level, but a model with low SSC may still be FID-suboptimal for other reasons (limited model capacity, bad training data, etc.).

sections.heading: Adaptive Reheat is one specific online criterion.
sections.text: We test only one online criterion (RMS change in 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} across consecutive steps; Equation 23 ). Other online criteria—score-norm-based thresholds, step-size controllers, or learned reheat policies—might in principle outperform ours. We do not test these and view them as complementary future work. However, we note that any online criterion incurs the additional NFE overhead of evaluating the criterion itself, which our results show DDIM does not need.

Muhammad Haris Khan Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Copenhagen, Denmark Correspondence to: muhammad.kahn@di.ku.dk Abstract Diffusion models generate samples by iteratively denoising a Gaussian prior, traversing a sequence of noise levels that, in every published sampler, decreases monotonically. Six years of intensive work has refined nearly every aspect of this recipe — the corruption operator, the training objective, the schedule shape, the architecture, and the ODE solver — yet the assumption of monotonicity itself has never been systematically tested. Here we ask whether monotonic sampling is load-bearing or merely conventional. We design four families of structured non-monotonic schedules and apply them to three architecturally distinct generative models — DDPM, EDM and Flow Matching — across NFE budgets ranging from 10 10 to 200 200 function evaluations, plus a 42 42 -cell hyperparameter ablation, on CIFAR-10. Across all 90 90 tested configurations, no tested non-monotonic schedule improves on the monotonic baseline. The magnitude of the penalty, however, spans nearly three orders of magnitude: persistent and substantial in DDPM, intermediate in Flow Matching, and indistinguishable from zero in EDM. We show that this variation is not noise but a structural property of each trained denoiser, and we formalise it as the Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient — a cheap, architecture-agnostic diagnostic that provides evidence of non-convergence to the Bayes-optimal denoiser at the critical noise level. Our findings justify the field’s tacit reliance on monotonic schedules and supply a new probe of diffusion-model quality complementary to sample-quality metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance. Keywords: Diffusion models, Generative modeling, Noise schedule, Sampling algorithms, Empirical evaluation, Denoising diffusion probabilistic models, Flow matching. 1 Introduction Every diffusion sampler in widespread use today—DDIM, DDPM, EDM with Heun integration, DPM-Solver, UniPC, the Euler and stochastic flow-matching samplers—shares a single, unstated structural assumption: the noise level decreases monotonically along the sampling trajectory . A schedule in which σ ^ τ i \hat{\sigma}_{\tau_{i}} is strictly decreasing in i i is treated as a definitional property of the reverse process, not as a design choice. This monotonicity assumption has remained a silent default for the roughly six years since the publication of DDPM, despite the field’s otherwise exhaustive ablation of nearly every other design dimension: the corruption operator ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Daras et al., 2023b ; Hoogeboom & Salimans, 2023 ) , the parametrisation ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , the training objective and weighting ( Kingma et al., 2021 ; Hang et al., 2023 ) , the variance schedule shape ( Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ; Chen, 2023 ) , the model architecture ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Karras et al., 2024b ) , and the sampling solver ( Lu et al., 2022a ; Zhang & Chen, 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . What has not been studied is whether the trajectory must move monotonically in the first place. Three independent threads of evidence suggest the question is non-trivial. First, the DDIM update equation ( Song et al., 2021a ) is mathematically well-defined for any choice of next-timestep τ i + 1 \tau_{i+1} , with no restriction to τ i + 1 < τ i \tau_{i+1}<\tau_{i} ( Proposition 1 ). Second, stochastic DDPM sampling already performs an implicit form of reheating: at every step it adds fresh Gaussian noise that partially counteracts the denoising progress made in the same step, and at high NFE this stochastic “churn” yields measurably better FID than deterministic DDIM ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . Third, Restart Sampling ( Xu et al., 2023 ) explicitly injects a large block of noise mid-trajectory and reports state-of-the-art quality when paired with deterministic correction. Taken together, these observations leave open a basic question that the literature has not answered: if diffusion samplers are mathematically permitted to step backward along the noise schedule, and if both stochastic DDPM and Restart Sampling appear to benefit from doing so, then is monotonicity merely a historical convention—something we could relax for free, or even profit from? By analogy to annealing-style escape—a heuristic familiar from non-convex optimisation, where occasional uphill steps allow an iterative procedure to leave poor local optima—one might hypothesise that structured reheating , i.e. deliberate non-monotonic increases in σ ^ \hat{\sigma} during sampling, should help the sampler escape suboptimal trajectories and reach better samples. This hypothesis is consistent with every piece of evidence cited above. Yet it has never been tested. We test it. We design four families of structured non-monotonic schedules ( Figure 4 ): Single Reheat , a single backward step of magnitude δ \delta at position t reheat t_{\text{reheat}} ; Sawtooth , periodic reheats of equal magnitude; Damped Oscillation , geometrically decaying reheats concentrated at the critical noise level log ⁡ SNR ≈ 0 \log\mathrm{SNR}\approx 0 identified by Hang et al. (2024) as governing perceptual quality; and Adaptive Reheat , an online schedule that triggers reheating when consecutive score predictions diverge. For the three fixed-budget non-adaptive families (Single Reheat, Sawtooth, Damped Oscillation), the total NFE budget remains fixed and matches the monotonic baseline—reheats are inserted within the budget, not added on top of it. Adaptive Reheat is the one exception: it adds reheat steps online up to a cap of 15 15 , and we report both fixed-NFE and time-matched comparisons for it ( Section 4.2 ). We evaluate all four families against monotonic DDIM on three architecturally distinct model families: DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , on CIFAR-10, across NFE budgets from 10 10 to 200 200 . A 42-configuration grid search over ( t reheat , δ ) (t_{\text{reheat}},\delta) provides exhaustive ablation. Two findings emerge, one negative and one positive. The negative finding is that reheating never helps. Across 48 schedule–budget combinations and the 42-cell ablation, no tested non-monotonic configuration improves upon the monotonic baseline on any model family at any NFE budget ( Figures 3 and 2 , Table 1 ). The penalty is monotonically increasing in reheat magnitude δ \delta at every reheat position, with no local minimum below zero. The result is robust: it holds for explicit single-reheat schedules, for periodic and damped-oscillation schedules, for an online adaptive criterion, and for both deterministic and stochastic-corrected variants. The positive finding—and the paper’s main contribution—is that while reheating uniformly hurts, the magnitude of the penalty is sharply, predictably, and architecture-dependent . At NFE = 100, the damped-oscillation schedule produces a + 1.31 +1.31 FID penalty on DDPM that has not converged toward zero even at the highest budget tested; a + 0.04 +0.04 FID penalty on Flow Matching, an order of magnitude smaller; and a − 0.003 -0.003 FID change on EDM—statistically indistinguishable from zero at the noise floor of FID-25K ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ). The penalty thus spans nearly three orders of magnitude across model families that achieve roughly tenfold-different baseline FID. This is not noise: the gap is consistent across NFE budgets, schedule types, and reheat magnitudes. We bound the per-reheat-step squared displacement by K 1 ​ L t 2 ​ ε 2 ​ ( σ ^ i ) + K 2 ​ ε 2 ​ ( σ ^ ′ ) K_{1}\,L^{2}_{t}\,\varepsilon^{2}(\hat{\sigma}_{i})+K_{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}(\hat{\sigma}^{\prime}) , where L t L_{t} is the local Lipschitz constant of the trained denoiser at the reheated noise level and ε \varepsilon is the per-noise-level denoiser error ( Proposition 2 ); for small reheats this reduces to a linear-in- δ \delta FID penalty whose slope is L t ⋅ ε ⁡ ( σ ^ i ) L_{t}\cdot\varepsilon(\hat{\sigma}_{i}) ( Section 5 ). A reheat step re-corrupts the sampler’s current best estimate 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} and demands the denoiser re-process it; for a Bayes-optimal denoiser this second pass extracts no additional information and the step is a wasted NFE. For an imperfect denoiser, errors accumulate non-trivially, and the larger L t L_{t} , the more they amplify. The penalty therefore measures, in a single architecture-agnostic scalar, how far the trained denoiser sits from the Bayes-optimal one at the perturbed noise level. We formalise this as the Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC; Definition 3 ): SSC \displaystyle\mathrm{SSC} ≔ lim N → ∞ [ Δ ​ FID DO ​ ( N ) ] + [ Δ ​ FID SR ​ ( N ) ] + , \displaystyle\coloneqq\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{DO}}(N)]_{+}}{[\Delta\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{SR}}(N)]_{+}}, (1) [ x ] + \displaystyle[x]_{+} ≔ max ⁡ ( x , 0 ) . \displaystyle\coloneqq\max(x,0). estimated empirically at NFE = 100. Table 3 reports SSC values of 1.83 1.83 for DDPM, 0.12 0.12 for Flow Matching, and ≈ 0 \approx\!0 for EDM, in tight rank-correlation with each model’s baseline FID. SSC is cheap: a full estimate requires two 256 256 -sample generation runs, totalling roughly ten minutes of compute on a single consumer GPU. Our negative finding is not that all forms of non-monotonicity fail. Stochastic DDPM at NFE = 200 outperforms deterministic DDIM on our benchmark ( Figure 3 b)—an empirical fact our analysis explains, not contradicts. The stochastic update decomposes into a parallel component (noise-cancelling, an implicit reheat) and an orthogonal component (trajectory diversification on the data manifold), and the orthogonal component drives the gain at high NFE ( Section 3.6 ). Our structured, deterministic reheating schedules operate purely in the parallel direction and therefore cannot replicate this benefit. The clarification cuts in the other direction as well: prior work informally cites RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) as evidence that reheating helps in general. We show that RePaint’s gains depend on per-step conditioning anchors that are unavailable in unconditional generation, and that pure reheating without anchoring or correction is uniformly harmful ( Section 2 ). Our contributions are: 1. The first systematic empirical test of monotonicity in diffusion sampling, covering three model families, four schedule types, NFE budgets ranging from 10–200, and a 42-cell ablation. Zero of the tested non-monotonic configurations improves on the monotonic baseline. 2. Evidence that the reheating penalty varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across DDPM, Flow Matching, and EDM, and is a structural property of the trained denoiser rather than measurement noise. 3. The Schedule Sensitivity Coefficient (SSC), with a proof that SSC > 0 \mathrm{SSC}>0 implies non-Bayes-optimal denoising at the critical noise level ( Proposition 3 ). SSC is cheap, architecture-agnostic, and complementary to FID. 4. Resolution of two community confusions: the relationship between explicit reheating and DDPM stochasticity ( Section 3.6 ), and the apparent contradiction between our finding and RePaint ( Section 2 ). Section 2 situates the work in the diffusion-sampling literature; Section 3 formalises non-monotonic schedules and proves their validity; Section 4 reports the empirical study; Section 5 develops the bounds and defines SSC; and Section 7 discusses limitations and open questions. 2 Related Work Diffusion and flow-matching generative models share a structural assumption that no canonical sampler we are aware of relaxes: the noise level decreases monotonically along the sampling trajectory. We position our contribution against four threads of prior work and, at the end of each, indicate the gap our paper fills. Foundational families and schedule design. Modern denoising diffusion descends from Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) and the practical recipe of Ho et al. (2020) (DDPM), which fixed a linear β \beta -schedule and a Markov reverse process whose variance shrinks monotonically toward t = 0 t=0 . Song et al. (2021a) (DDIM) reinterpreted the chain as a deterministic non-Markovian process; Song et al. (2021b) unified DDPM and the score networks of Song & Ermon (2019) ; Song & Ermon (2020) under a continuous-time SDE/ODE with strictly decreasing σ ⁡ ( t ) \sigma(t) ; Karras et al. (2022) (EDM) recast sampling as Heun integration over a strictly monotonic σ \sigma -schedule. Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and Stochastic Interpolants ( Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2023 ) integrate a velocity field along a monotone probability path, and Esser et al. (2024) scaled rectified-flow transformers (SD3) for high-resolution synthesis. Architecture work — Karras et al. (2024b) (EDM2), Peebles & Xie (2023) (DiT), Rombach et al. (2022) (Latent Diffusion) — inherits the scheduling assumption. A large body of work then optimises the shape of the monotonic schedule: the cosine schedule ( Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ) , the learnable VDM ( Kingma et al., 2021 ) , resolution-dependent logSNR shifts ( Chen, 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ) , Min-SNR ( Hang et al., 2023 ) and importance sampling around log ⁡ SNR = 0 \log\mathrm{SNR}=0 ( Hang et al., 2024 ) , terminal-SNR fixes ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , solver-aware step placement ( Sabour et al., 2024 ) , weighted-ELBO objectives ( Kingma & Gao, 2023 ) , and SNR refinements in HDiT ( Crowson et al., 2024 ) . Every entry above optimises within the space of monotonic schedules. We instead ask whether monotonicity is necessary at all, and provide the first systematic empirical answer. Inference-time algorithms. Fast deterministic solvers reduce NFE while preserving quality: DPM-Solver and DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2022a ; Lu et al., 2022b ) , exponential integrators ( Zhang & Chen, 2023 ) , the predictor-corrector UniPC ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , and DPM-Solver-v3 ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . All preserve monotonicity between function evaluations. The closest precedent to our schedules is Restart Sampling ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , which injects noise mid-trajectory paired with deterministic correction back to the pre-injection noise level. On the stochastic side, DDPM’s η = 1 \eta=1 sampler and the S churn S_{\text{churn}} parameter of Karras et al. (2022) inject infinitesimal in-step noise whose net trajectory remains monotone in expectation. Inference-time control techniques manipulate the trajectory without retraining: classifier guidance ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , and autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024a ) . Most directly relevant is RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , which reheats while conditioning on known pixels at every step; the unmasked region acts as a per-step anchor that pins the trajectory to a specific data point. We deliberately strip out the corrector, the conditioning, and the per-step anchor, isolating the effect of pure non-monotonic noise injection. Our negative result clarifies that Restart’s gains come from the corrector, that DDPM’s gains come from orthogonal diversification ( S churn / η S_{\text{churn}}/\eta does not capture macroscopic non-monotonicity), and that RePaint’s gains come from the conditioning rather than from the reheat. Departures from canonical assumptions. A small but influential lineage challenges diffusion’s universal assumptions. Bansal et al. (2023) (Cold Diffusion) replace Gaussian noise with deterministic degradations; Daras et al. (2023b) (Soft Diffusion) generalise the corruption operator to any linear process and explicitly note that monotonicity is not theoretically required, though they do not test non-monotonic schedules empirically; Hoogeboom & Salimans (2023) and Rissanen et al. (2023) build generative models from blur alone. These works vary the forward corruption; we hold the forward process fixed and vary only the reverse-time schedule , providing the systematic empirical test that Daras et al. (2023b) flagged but did not run. Denoiser quality and evaluation. Vincent (2011) established the score-matching/denoising equivalence underlying all diffusion training, and Song & Ermon (2019) observed that score quality is heterogeneous across noise levels. Karras et al. (2024b) diagnose architectural pathologies of the denoiser, and Daras et al. (2023a) train a consistency loss that penalises exactly the off-trajectory drift our SSC measures — their training objective amounts to driving SSC toward zero. Sample quality is canonically measured by FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) ; Sajjadi et al. (2018) and Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) introduced precision/recall variants for fidelity vs. coverage. These metrics evaluate outputs but offer little insight into why a model succeeds or fails. SSC is a behavioural probe complementary to FID : by measuring how much FID degrades under a controlled non-monotonic perturbation, it reveals the implicit assumptions a trained denoiser has baked in about its sampling trajectory. 3 Method We test the necessity of monotonic noise schedules by constructing four families of structured non-monotonic schedules, applied to three architecturally distinct generative model families: a discrete-time DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , a continuous- σ \sigma EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , and a flow-matching model ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Because each family parameterises its sampling trajectory differently (integer timestep, continuous noise level, and continuous time respectively), we describe the three samplers separately ( Sections 3.1 , 3.2 and 3.3 ) before introducing the unified definition of a reheat step ( Section 3.4 ) and the four schedule families ( Section 3.5 ).
